Pathology-03.question: ১) Ascariasis is caused by which of the following parasite?
Pathology-03.exp:
The correct answer is Ascaris lumbricoides. Ascariasis is an intestinal helminthic infection caused by the roundworm Ascaris lumbricoides, transmitted through ingestion of eggs from contaminated food or soil.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Necator americanus – Causes hookworm infection, leading to iron deficiency anaemia.

  • Ancylostoma duodenale – Also causes hookworm disease.

  • Strongyloides stercoralis – Causes strongyloidiasis, which may cause hyperinfection in immunosuppressed patients.

High-yield points:

Common intestinal helminths:

Parasite Disease
Ascaris lumbricoides Ascariasis
Ancylostoma/Necator Hookworm
Strongyloides stercoralis Strongyloidiasis
Enterobius vermicularis Pinworm infection

Exam pearl:
Ascariasis = Ascaris lumbricoides.

Pathology-03.question: ২) Humans are infected by Ascaris lumbricoides through which of the following route?
Pathology-03.exp:
The correct answer is oral route. Humans acquire Ascaris lumbricoides infection by ingestion of embryonated eggs present in contaminated food, water, or soil.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Blood – Ascaris larvae migrate through the bloodstream during the life cycle, but this is not the route of entry.

  • Skin penetration – Seen in hookworm (Ancylostoma, Necator) and Strongyloides infections.

  • Fecal – Eggs are passed in faeces, but infection occurs after ingestion of contaminated material, not directly by faecal route.

High-yield points:

Ascaris life cycle:

  1. Eggs ingested orally

  2. Larvae hatch in intestine

  3. Migrate via portal circulation → liver → lungs

  4. Ascend trachea → swallowed

  5. Mature into adult worms in small intestine

Exam pearl:
Ascaris infection = Oral ingestion of embryonated eggs.

Pathology-03.question: ৩) CBC finding of ascariasis is
Pathology-03.exp:
The correct answer is eosinophilia. Ascariasis, like other helminthic infections, commonly causes peripheral eosinophilia due to an immune response against the parasite, especially during the larval migration phase through tissues.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Neutropenia – Not a typical finding in parasitic infections.

  • Monocytosis – Seen in some chronic infections and inflammatory conditions, but not characteristic of ascariasis.

  • Lymphocytosis – More commonly associated with viral infections.

High-yield points:

Helminthic infection → Eosinophilia

  • Ascariasis

  • Hookworm infection

  • Strongyloidiasis

  • Schistosomiasis

Ascaris lung migration:

  • Causes Löffler syndrome

  • Features:

    • Transient pulmonary infiltrates

    • Cough

    • Eosinophilia

Exam pearl:
Ascariasis + CBC = Eosinophilia.

Pathology-03.question: ৪) Ancylostomiasis is caused by which of the following?
Pathology-03.exp:
The correct answer is Necator americanus. Ancylostomiasis (hookworm infection) is caused by hookworms, mainly Necator americanus and Ancylostoma duodenale.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Ascaris lumbricoides – Causes ascariasis.

  • Strongyloides stercoralis – Causes strongyloidiasis.

  • Enterobius vermicularis – Causes enterobiasis (pinworm infection).

High-yield points:

Hookworm infection:

  • Organisms:

    • Necator americanus

    • Ancylostoma duodenale

  • Route of entry → Skin penetration

  • Major complication → Iron deficiency anaemia

  • CBC finding → Eosinophilia

Exam pearl:
Ancylostomiasis = Hookworm = Necator americanus / Ancylostoma duodenale.

Pathology-03.question: ৫) Humans are infected by Hookworms through which of the following route?
Pathology-03.exp:
The correct answer is skin penetration. Hookworms (Ancylostoma duodenale and Necator americanus) infect humans when filariform larvae penetrate intact skin, usually through bare feet while walking on contaminated soil.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Oral – Typical route for Ascaris lumbricoides and some other intestinal parasites.

  • Blood – Larvae migrate through the bloodstream after entry but this is not the route of infection.

  • Fecal – Eggs are passed in faeces, but infection occurs by larval skin penetration.

High-yield points:

Hookworm life cycle:

  1. Eggs passed in stool

  2. Larvae develop in soil

  3. Filariform larvae penetrate skin

  4. Bloodstream → lungs → trachea → swallowed

  5. Adults attach to small intestine and cause blood loss

Exam pearl:
Hookworm infection = Skin penetration → Iron deficiency anaemia.

Pathology-03.question: ৬) What is the x-ray finding of Ancylostomiasis?
Pathology-03.exp:
The correct answer is consolidation. During the pulmonary migration phase of Ancylostomiasis (hookworm infection), larvae pass through the lungs and may cause transient pulmonary infiltrates/consolidation with eosinophilia, similar to Löffler syndrome.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Collapse – Seen in conditions causing airway obstruction (e.g., tumour, mucus plug), not typical of hookworm.

  • Cavitation – Commonly associated with tuberculosis, abscess, and some fungal infections.

  • Hilar lymphadenopathy – Seen in tuberculosis, lymphoma, and sarcoidosis.

High-yield points:

Hookworm pulmonary phase:

  • Larval migration through lungs

  • Transient infiltrates on chest X-ray

  • Eosinophilia

  • Cough/wheeze

Exam pearl:
Ancylostomiasis → Löffler syndrome → transient pulmonary consolidation + eosinophilia.

Pathology-03.question: ৭) What is the first line treatment of Ancylostomiasis?
Pathology-03.exp:
The correct answer is Albendazole. Albendazole is the first-line treatment for ancylostomiasis (hookworm infection) due to its broad-spectrum activity against intestinal helminths.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Ivermectin – First-line treatment for strongyloidiasis.

  • Mebendazole – Also effective against hookworm, but generally considered an alternative.

  • Pyrantel pamoate – Used mainly for Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm) and some other intestinal nematodes.

High-yield points:

Hookworm (Ancylostoma/Necator):

  • Treatment → Albendazole

  • Complication → Iron deficiency anaemia

  • Route of infection → Skin penetration

  • CBC → Eosinophilia

Exam pearl:
Ancylostomiasis = Albendazole (first line).

Pathology-03.question: ৮) Which public health measure should be taken to prevent hookworm infection?
Pathology-03.exp:
The correct answer is wear shoes. Hookworm infection occurs when filariform larvae penetrate the skin, commonly through bare feet while walking on contaminated soil. Wearing shoes prevents direct skin contact and reduces infection risk.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Hand washing – Important for preventing fecal–oral infections (e.g., ascariasis, enterobiasis), but less effective for hookworm.

  • Vaccination – No licensed vaccine is available for hookworm infection.

  • Community chemotherapy – May reduce prevalence in endemic areas, but the key individual preventive measure is avoiding skin penetration by wearing footwear.

High-yield points:

Hookworm prevention:

  • Wear shoes (most important)

  • Proper sanitation and disposal of faeces

  • Avoid soil contamination

  • Periodic deworming in endemic communities

Exam pearl:
Hookworm enters through skin → Wear shoes prevents infection.

Pathology-03.question: ৯) Which plasmodium species causes most serious disease?
Pathology-03.exp:
The correct answer is Plasmodium falciparum. It causes the most severe and life-threatening form of malaria due to its ability to invade all ages of red blood cells and cause cytoadherence and sequestration of infected RBCs in small blood vessels.

Complications include:

  • Cerebral malaria

  • Severe anaemia

  • Renal failure

  • Hypoglycaemia

  • Shock

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Plasmodium vivax – Common worldwide and can cause relapse due to dormant liver hypnozoites, but usually causes less severe disease.

  • Plasmodium ovale – Causes relatively mild malaria with relapse potential.

  • Plasmodium malariae – Usually causes mild chronic infection; associated with quartan fever.

High-yield points:

Malaria species:

Species Key feature
P. falciparum Most severe malaria; cerebral malaria
P. vivax Relapse due to hypnozoites
P. ovale Relapse; mild disease
P. malariae Quartan fever

Exam pearl:
Most serious malaria = Plasmodium falciparum.

Pathology-03.question: ১০) Which of the following is the vector of Plasmodia?
Pathology-03.exp:
The correct answer is Anopheles mosquito. Plasmodium species, the causative organisms of malaria, are transmitted by the bite of the female Anopheles mosquito.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Culex quinquefasciatus – Vector of filariasis (e.g., Wuchereria bancrofti) and other diseases.

  • Aedes aegypti – Vector of dengue, chikungunya, yellow fever, and Zika virus.

  • Sand fly – Vector of leishmaniasis.

High-yield points:

Malaria transmission:

  • Vector → Female Anopheles mosquito

  • Parasite → Plasmodium

  • Infective stage to humans → Sporozoite

  • Infective stage to mosquito → Gametocyte

Exam pearl:
Plasmodium vector = Female Anopheles mosquito.

Pathology-03.question: ১১) Which of the following plasmodium species may persist in liver cells as dormant forms?
Pathology-03.exp:
The correct answer is Plasmodium ovale. P. ovale can persist in liver cells as dormant forms called hypnozoites, which can reactivate later and cause relapse.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Plasmodium knowlesi – Causes malaria in humans but does not form hypnozoites.

  • Plasmodium malariae – May persist for years in blood but does not have dormant liver forms.

  • Plasmodium falciparum – Causes severe malaria but does not form hypnozoites.

High-yield points:

Hypnozoite-forming Plasmodium species:

  • P. vivax

  • P. ovale

Relapse due to hypnozoites → requires primaquine/tafenoquine for radical cure.

Exam pearl:
Dormant liver stage (hypnozoite) = P. vivax & P. ovale.

Pathology-03.question: ১২) In which of the following species of plasmodium inefection, fever comes in every alternate days?
১৩) rk39 is done for the diagnosis of which of the following?
Pathology-03.exp:
The correct answer is kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis). rK39 immunochromatographic test detects antibodies against the recombinant K39 antigen of Leishmania donovani and is used for rapid diagnosis of visceral leishmaniasis.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Malaria – Diagnosed by peripheral blood film (PBF) or rapid antigen tests detecting Plasmodium antigens.

  • Typhoid – Diagnosed by blood culture or serological tests such as Widal test (with limitations).

  • Tuberculosis – Diagnosed by AFB smear, GeneXpert, culture, or molecular tests.

High-yield points:

Kala-azar (Visceral leishmaniasis):

  • Organism → Leishmania donovani

  • Vector → Sand fly (Phlebotomus)

  • Diagnostic test → rK39

  • Features:

    • Prolonged fever

    • Massive splenomegaly

    • Pancytopenia

    • Hypergammaglobulinaemia

Exam pearl:
rK39 test = Kala-azar (Visceral leishmaniasis).

Pathology-03.question: ১৪) Which drug is used for prevention of malaria?
Pathology-03.exp:
The correct answer is doxycycline. Doxycycline is used for malaria chemoprophylaxis, especially for travellers visiting areas with chloroquine-resistant Plasmodium falciparum.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Co-artemether (artemether-lumefantrine) – Used for treatment of uncomplicated falciparum malaria, not routine prevention.

  • Artesunate – Used in the treatment of severe malaria (usually with another antimalarial), not prophylaxis.

  • Quinine – Used for treatment of severe or complicated malaria, not routine prevention.

High-yield points:

Malaria prophylaxis drugs:

  • Doxycycline

  • Atovaquone-proguanil

  • Mefloquine

  • Chloroquine (where sensitive)

Exam pearl:
Malaria prevention = Doxycycline (common prophylactic drug).

Pathology-03.question: ১৫) Type 1 diabetes mellitus is associated with which type of hypersensitivity?
Pathology-03.exp:
The correct answer is Type IV hypersensitivity. Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) is an autoimmune T-cell mediated disease in which cytotoxic T lymphocytes destroy pancreatic β-cells, leading to insulin deficiency.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Type I – IgE-mediated immediate hypersensitivity (e.g., asthma, anaphylaxis).

  • Type II – Antibody-mediated cytotoxic reaction (e.g., autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, Graves’ disease). Although autoantibodies may be present in T1DM, β-cell destruction is primarily T-cell mediated.

  • Type III – Immune complex-mediated disease (e.g., SLE).

High-yield points:

Type of hypersensitivity:

Type Mechanism Examples
I IgE + mast cells Asthma, anaphylaxis
II IgG/IgM against cells Graves’ disease, autoimmune haemolysis
III Immune complexes SLE
IV T-cell mediated T1DM, TB, contact dermatitis

Exam pearl:
Type 1 diabetes mellitus = Type IV (T-cell mediated autoimmune destruction of β-cells).

Pathology-03.question: ১৬) Which of the following is the vector of visceral leishmaniasis?
Pathology-03.exp:
The correct answer is sandfly. Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) is transmitted by the bite of the female sandfly (Phlebotomus species), which acts as the vector for Leishmania donovani.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Culex quinquefasciatus – Vector of lymphatic filariasis (Wuchereria bancrofti).

  • Aedes aegypti – Vector of dengue, chikungunya, yellow fever, and Zika virus.

  • Anopheles – Vector of malaria (Plasmodium species).

High-yield points:

Visceral leishmaniasis (Kala-azar):

  • Organism → Leishmania donovani

  • Vector → Female sandfly (Phlebotomus)

  • Diagnostic test → rK39

  • Features:

    • Prolonged fever

    • Massive splenomegaly

    • Pancytopenia

    • Hypergammaglobulinaemia

Exam pearl:
Kala-azar vector = Sandfly.

Pathology-03.question: ১৭) CBC finding of Kala-azar is
Pathology-03.exp:
The classic CBC finding of kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis) is pancytopenia due to bone marrow suppression and hypersplenism.

Typical findings:

  • ↓ Haemoglobin → Anaemia

  • ↓ WBC → Leucopenia

  • ↓ Platelets → Thrombocytopenia

Among the given options, none represents the typical finding. If forced to choose, monocytosis may be considered because Leishmania is an intracellular parasite residing in macrophages/mononuclear phagocytes, but it is not the characteristic CBC finding.

Why other options are wrong:

  • Neutrophilia – Seen in bacterial infections, not kala-azar.

  • Eosinophilia – Common in helminthic infections, not visceral leishmaniasis.

  • Lymphocytosis – Common in some viral infections.

High-yield points:

Kala-azar (Visceral leishmaniasis):

  • Organism → Leishmania donovani

  • Vector → Sandfly

  • CBC → Pancytopenia

  • Due to → Hypersplenism + bone marrow involvement

  • Diagnostic test → rK39

Exam pearl:
Kala-azar + CBC = Pancytopenia (not eosinophilia).

Pathology-03.question: ১৮) Clinical feature of Giardiasis
Pathology-03.exp:
The correct answer is abdominal pain. Giardiasis is caused by Giardia lamblia and commonly presents with abdominal cramps/pain, bloating, flatulence, and foul-smelling greasy diarrhoea (steatorrhoea) due to malabsorption.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Fever – Not a typical feature of giardiasis.

  • Bloody diarrhoea – Suggests invasive intestinal infections (e.g., amoebiasis, bacterial dysentery), not giardiasis.

  • Constipation – Not a typical presentation.

High-yield points:

Giardiasis:

  • Organism → Giardia lamblia

  • Transmission → Feco-oral route (contaminated water/food)

  • Site → Duodenum and jejunum

  • Features:

    • Foul-smelling greasy diarrhoea

    • Abdominal cramps

    • Bloating and flatulence

    • Malabsorption

Exam pearl:
Giardiasis = Abdominal pain + greasy, foul-smelling diarrhoea.

Pathology-03.question: ১৯) ‘Malar rash’ is a characteristic feature of which of the following?
Pathology-03.exp:
The correct answer is Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). A malar rash (butterfly rash) is a classic feature of SLE, characterized by erythema over the cheeks and bridge of the nose while typically sparing the nasolabial folds.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) – Characterized by inflammatory polyarthritis, rheumatoid nodules, and extra-articular features, but not malar rash.

  • Systemic sclerosis – Causes skin thickening, Raynaud phenomenon, and sclerodactyly.

  • Osteoarthritis – A degenerative joint disease without autoimmune skin manifestations.

High-yield points:

SLE features:

  • Malar rash

  • Photosensitivity

  • Oral ulcers

  • Arthritis

  • Serositis

  • Renal involvement

  • Anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm antibodies

Exam pearl:
Butterfly (malar) rash = SLE.

Pathology-03.question: ২০) SLE is associated with which type of hypersensitivity?
Pathology-03.exp:
The correct answer is Type III hypersensitivity. Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is primarily an immune complex-mediated disease. Antigen–antibody complexes deposit in tissues, activating complement and causing inflammation.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Type I – IgE-mediated immediate hypersensitivity (e.g., asthma, anaphylaxis).

  • Type II – Antibody-mediated cytotoxic reactions (e.g., autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, Graves’ disease). Some SLE manifestations like haemolytic anaemia involve Type II mechanisms, but the overall disease is Type III.

  • Type IV – T-cell mediated delayed hypersensitivity (e.g., tuberculosis, contact dermatitis, type 1 diabetes mellitus).

High-yield points:

Type Mechanism Examples
I IgE + mast cells Asthma, anaphylaxis
II IgG/IgM against cells Graves’ disease, autoimmune haemolysis
III Immune complex deposition SLE, serum sickness
IV T-cell mediated TB, contact dermatitis

Exam pearl:
SLE = Type III hypersensitivity (immune complex disease).

Pathology-03.question: ২১) Which of the following is pathognomonic hallmark of gout?
Pathology-03.exp:
The correct answer is tophi. Tophi (deposits of monosodium urate crystals) are considered the hallmark/pathognomonic feature of chronic gout. They represent accumulation of urate crystals surrounded by inflammatory granulomatous tissue.

Common sites:

  • Pinna of ear

  • Fingers

  • Toes

  • Olecranon bursa

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Acute arthritis – Common presentation of gout (podagra), but not pathognomonic.

  • Chronic tophaceous arthritis – A late manifestation of gout but not the specific hallmark lesion.

  • Gouty nephropathy – A complication due to urate deposition in kidneys.

High-yield points:

Gout:

  • Crystal → Monosodium urate

  • Site → Joint/synovial fluid

  • Acute attack → Podagra (1st MTP joint)

  • Diagnostic finding → Needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals

  • Hallmark lesion → Tophi

Exam pearl:
Gout + pathognomonic finding = Tophi (monosodium urate deposits).

Pathology-03.question: ২২) Which type of cell is responsible for bone formation?
Pathology-03.exp:
The correct answer is osteoblasts. Osteoblasts are bone-forming cells responsible for synthesis of osteoid (organic bone matrix) and initiation of mineralization.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Osteoclasts – Responsible for bone resorption (bone breakdown).

  • WBC – White blood cells are involved in immunity, not bone formation.

  • RBC – Red blood cells transport oxygen and are produced in bone marrow.

High-yield points:

Bone cells:

Cell Function
Osteoblast Bone formation
Osteoclast Bone resorption
Osteocyte Mature bone cell, maintains bone matrix

Exam pearl:
Osteoblast = Builds bone; Osteoclast = Clears bone.

Pathology-03.question: ২৩) Biochemical feature of gout is?
Pathology-03.exp:
The correct answer is hyperuricemia. Gout occurs due to increased serum uric acid levels, leading to deposition of monosodium urate crystals in joints and tissues.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Hypocalcaemia – Not a feature of gout.

  • Hypokalaemia – Not associated with gout.

  • Hypernatraemia – Not a biochemical feature of gout.

High-yield points:

Gout:

  • Biochemical abnormality → Hyperuricemia

  • Crystal → Monosodium urate

  • Crystal shape → Needle-shaped

  • Birefringence → Strong negative birefringence

  • Common site → 1st metatarsophalangeal joint (podagra)

Exam pearl:
Gout = Hyperuricemia → monosodium urate crystal deposition.

Pathology-03.question: ২৪) Radiographic abnormalities of Rheumatoid arthritis is
Pathology-03.exp:
The correct answer is joint deformity. Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic inflammatory polyarthritis that causes progressive joint destruction and deformities due to synovial inflammation, pannus formation, cartilage destruction, and bone erosion.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Osteophytes – Typical of osteoarthritis (OA) due to degenerative changes.

  • Joint space narrowing – Can occur in RA due to cartilage loss, but it is not the most characteristic radiographic abnormality listed.

  • Subchondral sclerosis – A feature of osteoarthritis, not RA.

High-yield points:

X-ray findings in RA:

  • Soft tissue swelling

  • Periarticular osteopenia

  • Marginal erosions

  • Uniform joint space narrowing

  • Subluxation and joint deformities

X-ray findings in OA:

  • Osteophytes

  • Subchondral sclerosis

  • Cyst formation

  • Non-uniform joint space narrowing

Exam pearl:
RA → erosions + deformity; OA → osteophytes + sclerosis.

Pathology-03.question: ২৫) Which of the following is the hallmark of SLE?
Pathology-03.exp:
The correct answer is production of autoantibodies. The hallmark of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is the formation of multiple autoantibodies, especially:

  • Antinuclear antibodies (ANA) – highly sensitive

  • Anti-double stranded DNA (anti-dsDNA) – associated with lupus nephritis

  • Anti-Smith (anti-Sm) – highly specific

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Oral ulcer – A clinical feature of SLE but not the hallmark.

  • Joint hypermobility – Not a feature of SLE.

  • Skin rash – Common feature (e.g., malar rash), but not the defining hallmark.

High-yield points:

SLE:

  • Autoimmune connective tissue disease

  • Hallmark → Autoantibody production

  • Common antibodies:

    • ANA

    • Anti-dsDNA

    • Anti-Sm

  • Hypersensitivity → Type III (immune complex mediated)

Exam pearl:
SLE = autoantibody-mediated autoimmune disease.

Pathology-03.question: ২৬) ANA is 100% sensitive for which of the following disease?
Pathology-03.exp:
The correct answer is SLE (Systemic lupus erythematosus). Antinuclear antibody (ANA) is positive in almost all patients with SLE (≈95–100% sensitivity), making it a highly sensitive screening test.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Systemic sclerosis – ANA is positive in many patients, but not 100% sensitive.

  • Dermatomyositis – ANA may be positive but has lower sensitivity.

  • Rheumatoid arthritis – ANA is not a sensitive diagnostic marker; rheumatoid factor (RF) and anti-CCP are more relevant.

High-yield points:

Autoantibodies:

Disease Important antibody
SLE ANA (high sensitivity), anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm
Rheumatoid arthritis Anti-CCP, RF
Systemic sclerosis Anti-centromere, anti-Scl-70
Dermatomyositis Anti-Jo-1, anti-Mi-2

Exam pearl:
ANA positivity (~100% sensitivity) → SLE screening test.

Pathology-03.question: ২৭) Regarding giardiasis, which one is correct?
Pathology-03.exp:
The correct answer is malabsorption. Giardiasis (Giardia lamblia) affects the duodenum and jejunum, causing mucosal damage and impaired absorption, especially of fat, leading to steatorrhoea.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Fever – Not a typical feature of giardiasis.

  • Invasive – Giardiasis is a non-invasive intestinal infection.

  • Bloody diarrhoea – Suggests invasive infections such as amoebiasis or bacterial dysentery, not giardiasis.

High-yield points:

Giardiasis:

  • Organism → Giardia lamblia

  • Transmission → Feco-oral route

  • Site → Duodenum & jejunum

  • Nature → Non-invasive

  • Features:

    • Malabsorption

    • Foul-smelling greasy diarrhoea

    • Abdominal cramps

    • Bloating

Exam pearl:
Giardia = Non-invasive diarrhoea + malabsorption + steatorrhoea.

Pathology-03.question: ২৮) which of the following is the largest intestinal nematode ?
Pathology-03.exp:
The correct answer is Ascaris lumbricoides. It is the largest intestinal nematode (roundworm) infecting humans, with adult females reaching approximately 20–35 cm in length.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Necator americanus – Hookworm; much smaller (about 1 cm).

  • Ancylostoma duodenale – Hookworm; also small (about 1 cm).

  • Strongyloides stercoralis – Very small intestinal nematode (adult female about 2 mm).

High-yield points:

Important intestinal nematodes:

Parasite Key feature
Ascaris lumbricoides Largest intestinal nematode
Enterobius vermicularis Commonest intestinal nematode in many developed countries
Hookworm Causes iron deficiency anaemia
Strongyloides stercoralis Autoinfection, hyperinfection

Exam pearl:
Largest intestinal nematode = Ascaris lumbricoides.

Pathology-03.question: ২৯) Which protozoa infects all forms of RBC?
Pathology-03.exp:
The correct answer is Plasmodium falciparum. It is the only major human malaria parasite that can infect red blood cells of all ages (young, mature, and old RBCs), leading to high parasitaemia and severe disease.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • E. histolytica – Protozoa causing amoebiasis; infects intestinal mucosa, not RBCs.

  • T. cruzi – Causes Chagas disease; infects tissue cells, especially cardiac muscle and reticuloendothelial cells.

  • W. bancrofti – A filarial nematode causing lymphatic filariasis; not a protozoan and does not infect RBCs.

High-yield points:

RBC preference of Plasmodium:

Species RBC preference
P. falciparum All ages of RBCs
P. vivax Young RBCs (reticulocytes)
P. ovale Young RBCs (reticulocytes)
P. malariae Older RBCs

Exam pearl:
P. falciparum → infects RBCs of all ages → severe malaria.46674

Pathology-03.question: ৩০) Which of the following is the most common inflammatory arthritis in men?
Pathology-03.exp:
The correct answer is gout. Gout is the most common inflammatory arthritis in men, caused by deposition of monosodium urate crystals in joints due to hyperuricaemia.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Osteoarthritis – Most common overall arthritis, but it is a degenerative (non-inflammatory) arthritis.

  • Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) – Common inflammatory autoimmune arthritis, but it is more common in women.

  • Ankylosing spondylitis – Inflammatory arthritis affecting the axial skeleton, more common in young men, but less common than gout.

High-yield points:

Common arthritis facts:

  • Most common arthritis overall → Osteoarthritis

  • Most common inflammatory arthritis in men → Gout

  • Most common inflammatory polyarthritis → Rheumatoid arthritis

  • Most common spondyloarthritis → Ankylosing spondylitis

Exam pearl:
Male + inflammatory arthritis (most common) = Gout.
